rule: D53 (field subjects do not make trends persist; amends D13, D33)
trigger: data/reviews/subject-dupes-d48.json rechecks (cio-role, 'open'): Deloitte's recurring CIO chapter (2011-004, 2013-001, 2015-001) shares the capture's subject 'CIO role', so 2011-004 and 2013-001 were mechanically persisted and never rename-checked, while the D33 audit had already read the CIO-role link of 2014-001 as a field, not a trend.
sweep: Every row that scripts/trend-persistence.mjs computed as persisted at fc360b5, in all six trend sources, with the trend of the first next edition that shares its subject id (matched_in): accenture-tech-vision 0 pairs, a16z-big-ideas 0, deloitte-tech-trends 21, ftsg-tech-trends 1,315, mckinsey-tech-trends 36, trendwatching 5. Each pair was read on label, quote, note and position. Every pair whose two labels differ was read (Deloitte 16, FTSG 77, McKinsey 1, trendwatching 2), every pair whose shared label is one word (FTSG 127), and every Deloitte, McKinsey and trendwatching pair. Rule: a subject is a field subject only when the persisted pairs it creates assert different things about a broad topic (a role, a function, 'cyber', an umbrella against a specific application); a trend that continues under the same or a reworded name is not.
result: Two field subjects, both Deloitte Tech Trends: cio-role and cybersecurity. 5 persisted rows become rename candidates (pass 3, renames-d33-pass3-scope.json). No field subject in Accenture or a16z (no persisted rows), McKinsey (one trend list re-published yearly under the same names and definitions), trendwatching or FTSG (differing labels are spelling variants or the same trend; same-label pairs carry the same or updated text, and FTSG's own year tags count them as one trend, D40).
